articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Scream Sneeze?
articles.content:
Someone in my life who shall rename nameless (you know exactly who you are) is a scream sneezer. It is the loudest sneeze you’ve ever heard, and he manages to make it sound like he’s screaming AH SH*T—although he swears he’s not cursing on purpose. It’s so loud that it has woken our deaf dog out of a deep sleep, made more than one baby cry and set off a car alarm. I am not kidding. At this point, I’m less concerned about his sinuses than I am about whether our homeowners insurance covers sonic weapons.
Thus far, I have not punched him, but every sneeze startles me so badly that I fear the day is coming. I don’t want to be the first person convicted of assaulting someone for having a functioning respiratory system, but I also can’t comfortably rule it out.
If you’ve never been around a scream sneezer, I envy your innocence. They are a small but disproportionately terrifying percentage of the population, and once you’ve encountered one, your nervous system is permanently changed. You will forever brace yourself whenever someone in the vicinity inhales a little too deeply because a perfectly ordinary sneeze becomes a potential jump scare.
So, yes, scream sneezing is certainly alarming. And frustrating. And annoying. And an affront to “use your indoor voice.” But is it actually rude? After all, my loved one—yes, I still love him—swears that he isn’t trying to be so loud. He claims that his sneezes simply emerge dramatically, like a firework going off in a library. He swears he is not deliberately trying to frighten small children or make the dog question its place in the universe. I am not so sure.
Let’s chat about this.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
I am not the only person bothered by scream sneezes, and generally speaking, anything that makes a significant portion of the population want to throw a shoe at you deserves at least an etiquette investigation. So why does it feel so rude? Two factors: loudness and germs.
Scream sneezes aren’t just loud; they are loud loud. A study conducted by Noise Measurement Systems found that the average male sneeze is around 90 decibels when measured from 2 feet away. That’s roughly as loud as a blender running at full speed, except the blender has the decency to have a lid. The noise level does depend on the sneezer’s physiology—smaller lungs make quieter sneezes, for instance—so if the average is at 90 decibels, then scream sneezers could be entering jet-engine territory. So while I couldn’t find exact numbers for the volume of my loved one’s scream sneezes, I can report that he has made me question whether our windows are double-paned.
A sneeze is not merely a noise. It is a biological event involving a rapidly expelled mixture of droplets and particles and … other, potentially infectious, things. MIT researchers studying sneeze dynamics found that larger droplets can travel several feet, while smaller particles may travel up to 20 feet, depending on conditions. The exact distance depends on the sneeze and the surrounding environment, and we don’t know that a louder sneeze necessarily sends germs farther. Still, if someone is going to unleash a respiratory weather event in your direction, you would prefer they at least attempt to contain it.
A scream sneeze, then, combines two of the most universally disliked things in public life: an unnecessarily loud noise and the possibility of being involuntarily included in someone else’s germ-distribution system.
My loved one claims that because sneezing is a natural bodily function, it is exempt from etiquette. This is an interesting legal defense. I look forward to hearing him explain it to the next person who crop-dusts an elevator. Natural bodily functions are not, in fact, exempt from etiquette. We have rules about all sorts of them.
Etiquette does not require us to pretend our bodies don’t do strange things. It asks us to manage those things with reasonable consideration for everyone else.
Of course, not all bodily functions are equally controllable. Sneezing is a reflex, and trying to forcibly suppress a sneeze can actually be harmful, potentially damaging your eardrums and even rupturing blood vessels in extreme cases, according to the Cleveland Clinic. We should not expect anyone to achieve perfect control over something their body does without permission. But the question isn’t whether or not sneezing is rude—as long as you cover your mouth, you’re fine—but the screaming aspect of it.
I couldn’t find any research about how much control people have over the volume of their sneezes. Researchers have apparently been too busy studying important things like the trajectory of airborne pathogens to settle the disputes that actually matter to society. And I’m willing to entertain the possibility that some people genuinely cannot reduce the volume much. We all have different bodies, reflexes and medical circumstances.
But I also suspect that some scream sneezers have simply never considered whether they could do anything differently. When you’ve spent your entire life sneezing like a car backfiring, it may not occur to you that other people find it startling.
So, no, you cannot reasonably be expected to control what you genuinely cannot control. But you also can be reasonably expected to care about the effect you have on other people—especially when that effect may result in a mini cardiac event or a shower of germs.
My loved one scream sneezes straight into whatever or whoever is in front of him. He says the sneeze comes on so quickly that he can’t do anything about it. He also dislikes covering his mouth because then he gets snot on his hands. This is the part of his argument I find particularly compelling, in the sense that I find it compelling evidence that he has misunderstood the entire purpose of etiquette. He would rather distribute his mucus among innocent bystanders than briefly inconvenience himself.
A big part of scream sneezing is where it is happening and who is affected. For instance, if you’re at home by yourself, do whatever you like. But once others are around, especially if it’s in a crowded, public venue, that changes the noise calculus. It also matters who is around you. A scream sneeze is more consequential around sleeping babies, startled animals, people with sensory sensitivities or anyone who may be particularly vulnerable to respiratory infections.
Similar to the etiquette around telling someone you’re sick, the etiquette requirements here are not especially demanding.
I don’t know about you, but my first reaction when I’m startled is fear, anger and the desire to investigate whether I’m legally permitted to throw something. But punching the sneezer would definitely be rude—far ruder than the scream sneeze itself. It is also rude to shame someone, mock their medical circumstances or insist that they must be doing it on purpose. Even if you (and I) suspect that a person could control the volume at least somewhat, we cannot know what is happening inside their body. Offer grace … and perhaps a tissue.
If the behavior is genuinely affecting you, especially if the person repeatedly sneezes uncovered in your direction, it is reasonable to ask them to cover their mouth or turn away.
Scream sneezing is not inherently rude, but refusing to do anything to mitigate it is. While sneezing is a reflex, involuntary does not equal consequence-free. My ruling? The sneeze itself is innocent; the mucus distribution strategy is where things get legally interesting. My loved one, for instance, may be acquitted of the noise charge due to insufficient evidence of intent. But the charge of sneezing directly onto other people because he doesn’t want to get snot on his own hands? That case is going to trial.
And I would like the record to show that the dog is available as a witness.

articles.title: These Are the Most Popular Baby Names of 2026—Can You Guess What’s in the Top 10?
articles.content:
My brother and his wife just had a baby, and once we all got over our joy and elation that mom and baby were doing great, everyone’s attention turned to the name. What will it be? Will they go with a family name, a name that means something personal to them or maybe something pulled from a movie or trending TV show? I won’t spill it here, but my brother and his wife made a beautiful choice.
If you’re expecting a baby this year, or you’re just here to see what’s happening in the baby-naming world (why wouldn’t you be?), we have the top baby names of 2026 from the absolute authority: BabyCenter. I got the scoop from Steph Coffield, BabyCenter’s baby-name advisor, who breaks down the most popular names and lets us in on why these names are so big right now. Read on to squee over the top baby names of 2026.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more baby names, trends, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
These popular baby names come straight from mom and dad. “Hundreds of thousands of parents register their babies’ names on BabyCenter every year,” Coffield says. “That data is updated on our app and website every month, giving us an up-to-date look at which names are rising and falling.”
You may know that the Social Security Administration (SSA) puts out a list every year too, but Coffield says the SSA only updates its data once per year, and we won’t find out what 2026’s top baby names are until May 2027. “Our data gives parents an early look at what’s trending now, so they can make an informed decision about their baby’s name.”
For the fourth year in a row, Olivia and Noah are the reigning champs. Olivia has been steadily climbing for more than a quarter-century (she was sitting at No. 16 back in 2000), and it’s going to be hard to knock this pretty name off the top of the charts. Noah is equally enduring, taking the top spot from Liam in 2022 after being in the top 10 for years.
“Once a name makes it to the No. 1 spot, it usually sticks around for a while,” Coffield says. “Olivia and Noah are both beautiful names, which helps explain why they’ve been popular for so long.” Plus, Coffield says “parents have been really in love with vowel-heavy names for a few years now, and Olivia and Noah fit that bill.”
Evelyn is back, baby! This sweet name is at No. 9 this year after last being being spied in the top 10 in 2023. The rest of the girls’ top 10 is filled with familiar faces, though there was some jockeying for position.
For boys, Elias made the top 10 for the first time ever, rising 8 spots to sit at No. 7. The top 5 boys names have remained unchanged for three years, but Asher and Luca dropped out of the top 10 to make room for Elias and Leo, who was last seen in the top 10 in 2024.
Coffield says names starting with E are “super popular” this year—a full quarter of the top 20 girl names start with this letter. Case in point: Eliana, which made huge moves in 2026, jumping five spots to No. 2. Longer names are also surging, and soft-sounding names that end in vowels are still going strong. “Eliana has all of that: It’s long, soft, melodic and it starts with E. That’s why it’s having such a big moment this year.”
Here are the top 20 girl names for 2026:
This group doesn’t see as much movement as the girls’ list, but all of them would be perfect for your new baby. “Parents are a lot less experimental with boy names than with girl names, generally speaking,” Coffield says. “They’re more likely to choose a boy name that’s established, feels classic and will stand the test of time.”
Here are the top 20 boy names for 2026:
Oh, yeah. Several longtime faves are out of the top 100, including Leah and Ryan, and one brand-new name hit the charts: Magnolia, which jumped an impressive 40 spots to No. 88. Four boy names made the top 100 for the first time: Archer (No. 96), Stetson (No. 95), Milo (No. 89) and Dean, which sneaked in at No. 100 for the first time this century.
Coffield says these last three boy names each tap into a different trend. “Stetson is a rugged cowboy name that evokes the Wild West. Dean is having a pop-culture comeback, thanks to the characters on the new hit show Off Campus and the nostalgic classic Gilmore Girls. And Milo has that vowel-heavy, soft sound parents are loving right now.”
Longer names are also on the rise, with 29% of girl names and 31% of boy names clocking in at more than seven letters. “Baby-name trends are cyclical, and the pendulum always swings back,” Coffield says. “After a few years of short names dominating the charts, parents are looking for names that feel new and different, so they’re gravitating toward longer names.”
Pop culture has a major influence on baby-name trends, and next year, many parents will likely be borrowing from hit movies and must-see TV. Some of these baby names haven’t been heard in years! Here are some trends to watch for in 2027, according to Coffield and BabyCenter.

articles.title: Terror at 900 Feet: The Heart-Pounding Mission to Save Two People Trapped High Above Ground After a Hot-Air-Balloon Accident
articles.content:
Cliff Patrick’s shoulders, forearms and thighs burned with every step up to the next rung. He was climbing a 12-inch-wide ladder up the tallest communications tower in Longview, Texas—getting farther and farther from the security of the ground below. Once he got a couple hundred feet up, a disorienting visual effect set in. When Patrick looked down, he could no longer see the ground, and when he turned his gaze upward, he couldn’t see the sky. There was just an infinity of gray metal ladder in either direction.
On top of that, the 40-year-old firefighter carried the fear that at any moment he might see the basket of a hot-air balloon that had collided with the tower plummet past him with two people in it. If that happened, he would know he hadn’t climbed fast enough.
Rescue workers get called to crash sites all the time. That’s part of the job. But for Patrick and 13 other responders from the Longview Fire Department making their way up the tower, this crash site was 925 feet off the ground.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more true stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Rick James, 73, and Megan Reynolds, 38, had flown hot-air balloons together too many times to count. They had known each other since Reynolds was in grade school and her mother was on the board of directors at the Great Texas Balloon Race, which Longview hosts every summer.
James, an East Texas native and a longtime financial adviser with Morgan Stanley, began crewing for balloons in the race in 1980. In 2003, he took his hobby to the next level and got licensed as a balloon pilot. When he and Reynolds, a medical assistant for a dermatology practice in Marshall, Texas, lifted off around 7 a.m. on Saturday, Feb. 28, they were looking forward to a relaxing weekend soaring through the Texas skies.
James’s balloon, with its checkerboard pattern of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple and pink, was one of seven that launched together from an elementary school on the southeast side of Longview. The group planned to fly for a little over an hour in the gentle breeze, which was blowing at about 10 mph.
As James and Reynolds coasted along for the better part of an hour, they soaked in the beauty of the clear, mostly blue sky and shared a casual conversation. Floating 500 feet off the ground, they could hear dogs barking as the enormous balloons passed overhead.
Around 8 a.m., James started looking for an open area where they could land. In the distance, he saw the 1,098-foot FM radio tower—about the same height as New York City’s Chrysler Building—but he barely gave it a second thought. “I don’t have a place to land here—I’m just gonna fly over the tower,” James radioed to his eldest daughter, Lindsay, who, as part of his two-person chase crew, was tracking her dad’s movements from a van.
He turned the wooden handle of the propane-fueled burner, sending flames up into the canopy to ease the balloon upward. But as they ascended, the wind increased to 24 mph, pushing them hard toward the tower. James, unable to see the top of the tower because the balloon was blocking his view, was certain they’d be fine. “Right up until the last three or four seconds, I thought we were gonna clear the tower,” he says.
Then one side of the balloon collided with the crow’s nest, a small balcony jutting out from the triangular steel tower, puncturing the nylon fabric. The other side of the balloon wrapped itself around a guy wire stretching diagonally from the top of the tower to the ground. The impact of the collision knocked Reynolds to the floor of the basket, while James kept his balance by grabbing hold of one of the corner uprights. “Are you OK?” he asked her.
Reynolds paused to get her bearings. “Yeah, I think I skinned my leg a little bit, but I’m fine.”
They couldn’t see exactly what the balloon was hanging from. All they knew was that their brown wicker basket was lurching back and forth in the wind, about 10 feet from the side of the tower and terrifyingly high above the ground. They prayed that whatever was holding them up there wouldn’t release its grip.
Earlier that morning, Longview Fire Department Chief Jon-Eric Johnson, 41, sat down for breakfast with a co-worker. They tossed out hypotheticals, wondering what calls their shift that day might bring. Johnson saw a hot-air balloon drifting nearby and posited, “What if we go on a hot-air-balloon incident?”
Not more than 20 minutes later, the department’s dispatcher called Johnson’s cell. “Hey, we got a pretty serious event,” she said. “We think a hot-air balloon has crashed.” Witnesses on the ground, including James’s chase crew, were calling 911to report an unbelievable scene—a balloon had struck the communications tower. The details were all over the place. Some callers said the balloon was caught 100 feet up the tower, others said 500. Some said one person was in the basket; others said five.
Johnson got some answers for himself when he and his fellow rescue workers pulled out of the station. From 2 miles away, he could see, clear as day, James’s balloon snagged near the top.
Longview and the surrounding area are home to about 150 communications towers, so the fire department has rope-rescue experts on staff, including Cliff Patrick and his longtime friend Lt. Stephen Winchell. Patrick was at home, making pancakes for his three young kids, when he got a text from the department about a balloon accident.
He texted Johnson: “I can be there in about 30 minutes.” Johnson called and gave him the address. That’s when Patrick realized which tower Johnson was talking about. A rescue near the top of it had only ever been a hypothetical. Now it was reality.
As Reynolds sat in the basket, trying not to shift her weight and put additional strain on whatever was holding them there, James got to work. First, he shut off the balloon’s propane valves—there was no sense in keeping that dangerous gas flowing. Next, he realized he had to do something about the way the basket was swinging in the wind. He grabbed their drop line—a 150-foot rope that could be lowered to the chase crew to control the balloon’s landing—and around the end of it tied a handle, one similar to what a water-skier holds. Then he tossed the handle toward the tower. On the third attempt, it caught against one of the struts. James held on to the other end to steady the basket.
Every 10 minutes or so, the handle would come loose, and James would toss it over again. He didn’t mind the work—it occupied his mind and helped settle his nerves. Reynolds, too, was struggling to stay calm. “At first, it was sheer panic,” she says. From the bottom of the basket, she would occasionally hear the balloon’s fabric ripping, she remembers.
About 20 minutes after the balloon crashed into the tower, Johnson and his crew arrived with bolt cutters and cut through the padlocked perimeter fence around the tower. They forced entry into the building and killed the power—the tower had been pumping out 100,000 watts of electricity from its main antenna, just 43 feet above where the balloon was entangled.
Johnson got the phone numbers of the trapped balloonists from dispatch. He called James three times, but it kept going to voicemail. That’s because after James phoned his wife, Lori James, to tell her what had happened and to ask her to update their other kids, he started getting calls from other balloonists, and—not wanting to be distracted from the important work of steadying the basket—he had put the phone in his pocket and was ignoring it.
Next, Johnson called Reynolds, who picked up. “Hey, this is Chief Johnson,” he said. “We’re here. Can you tell me how many people are in the basket? Are you injured?” He got the key details from Reynolds, then asked to speak to James, who told the fire chief that he thought two of the four main cables between the basket and the balloon had broken. While they were talking, a third cable snapped. James and Reynolds felt the basket drop a few inches and swing wildly.
“Listen, we are coming for you,” Johnson said. “But I want to be honest. It’s probably gonna take about an hour to get to you.” That was an educated guess. None of his firefighters had ever climbed 925 feet before. None of them had ever climbed half that high.
With about 50 pounds of gear strapped to his back, including a 300-foot rope, Brayden Pointer was the first firefighter to start the climb up the tower, just before 9 a.m. At the same time, police drones were deployed to give the team a view of the crash site and take measurements: The vertical climb would be a little over 900 feet. Most of the rescue team’s ropes were 200 feet in length, so groups of two or three rescuers would have to be spaced out at precise spots on the tower. Their job: to lower the balloonists to the ground using pulleys and ropes.
Shortly after Pointer and four other firefighters started climbing up the tower, rope rescue specialists Patrick and Winchell arrived on the scene. They were given relatively little to carry so that they could get to the crash scene as quickly as possible. The climbers wore wide lanyards hooked to harnesses, allowing them to execute a technique known as clip climbing. Every couple of rungs, they had to reach down and undo one of two safety clips shaped something like lobster claws, then reach up and clip it to a higher rung. Step up, unclip, re-clip. Painstaking. Meticulous. Exhausting.
With his adrenaline pumping, Patrick quickly climbed the first 100 or so feet. Then fatigue set in. “I was probably stopping to shake out my forearms and shoulders every 50 or 60 feet after that,” he says. “And all the while, I was thinking about how to burn only 80% of my energy to get there, because I had to save 20% to actually make the rescue.”
To cut the tension as they climbed, Winchell hollered down to Patrick, “Have I ever told you I don’t love heights?” It was a joke based on the truth—Patrick knew that his climbing buddy had never fully gotten over his long-standing fear of heights. Winchell just worked around it, especially when lives were on the line.
On the ground, Capt. Ramey Blalock was given the job of talking to Reynolds on the phone. He stayed on the line with her for more than an hour. “I’m sure that Capt. Blalock got tired of me asking ‘Where are they?’ and ‘How long do you think it’s gonna be?’ ” Reynolds says. “But talking to him for the whole time kept me really calm.”
A little after 10 a.m., just as Pointer came into view 40 feet below the basket, James thought he felt the last of the main cables snap. “Look, we’re hanging only by fabric now,” he shouted to Pointer, who had stopped to catch his breath. “Please get up here and tie us off as soon as you can.”
Pointer powered through, got level with the basket and tied the balloon’s drop rope tight to the tower. Then he pulled a half-inch static kernmantle rope with a minimum breaking strength of 9,000 pounds from his pack and tossed one end to James, who tied it onto the basket while the firefighter secured the other end to the tower. With the rugged horizontal safety line in place, James got his barely suppressed panic under control. “That was the first time in two hours that I felt comfortable that I was not going to die,” he says.
Feeling more secure, Reynolds stood up, startling Pointer, who’d had no idea a second person was in the basket. “OK, I’m ready to get out now,” she declared before sitting back down.
Patrick and Winchell arrived soon after. The rescue workers clipped two harnesses to the rope that Pointer had established and slid them across to the basket. They gave James and Reynolds instructions for how to put the harnesses on, including cinching the leg hoops and buckling on the belts. Then Patrick climbed even higher and attached a second rescue rope to the tower 30 feet above the basket, so they could swing across like a pendulum. The firefighters hadn’t brought protective helmets for James and Reynolds, so Winchell and Patrick took off their own helmets and sent them across to the balloonists.
Next, Winchell, who later referred to this as the Super Bowl of rope rescue, climbed to the exterior of the tower and clipped in, ready to help James and Reynolds and to be, as he put it, “a human bumper if needed.” Given his fear of heights, he admits that he didn’t relish stepping onto the outer edge of the tower. “But it was clear to me what needed to be done,” he says. “I did what rescuers do every day: I turned down that voice in my head.”
James and Reynolds weren’t out of danger yet. If the basket ripped from the balloon and tipped over, they could still fall more than 900 feet to the ground below. Harnessed and helmeted, they were ready to embark on the high-wire ride of their lives. “Who wants to go first?” Winchell called across. Reynolds volunteered, and James agreed. “I felt responsible for putting Megan in this predicament,” he says.
Reynolds clipped the loop at the top of her harness to the high-point rope, which Patrick was manning, and sat backward on the edge of the basket. James held her feet and guided her out as she grabbed the horizontal rope, which stretched straight across to the tower. Refusing to look down, she swung on the high rope toward the tower in a seated position—sliding along, hand over hand on the horizontal rope to steady herself, all the while dangling 900 feet above the ground.
After what felt like an eternity (but was actually just a few seconds), Winchell was guiding her inside the metal structure. She unclipped from the rope and clipped onto the tower. “It was night and day once she got across,” Patrick recalls. “She thought she was gonna die in that basket, but once she got inside the tower, she was calm, collected, 100% able to follow commands.”
Next, it was James’s turn. He hooked his harness onto the line, stepped to the edge of the basket, turned his back to the tower and made his way across, his body swinging in the wind. Then Winchell grabbed hold of him and steered him into the tower. At 10:58 a.m., a little less than three hours after the balloon crashed, James and Reynolds were safe and secure, and thanking their rescuers profusely. But they still had 900 feet to go.
The firefighters’ plan was to lower James and Reynolds, still in their harnesses, a couple hundred feet at a time by hand, using ropes and pulleys. The rescuers agreed that the 73-year-old should get to the ground first, even though he was doing just fine physically. He also had family, including Lori and Lindsay, waiting below. The slow, careful descent began. At the first changeover point a couple hundred feet below, two firefighters hooked James into a safety clip attached to the tower, unclipped him from the first set of ropes and attached him to the second set.
“Have y’all ever done this before?” James asked the rescuers. “Yes,” came the response. “But not from this height.” Once James was on the second set of ropes, Reynolds began her descent. As the pair got closer to the ground, the mood turned lighter—at one of the stations, Capt. Clint Steelman told Reynolds he was hungry and asked if she had a cheeseburger.
Once James and Reynolds completed the transition off the first set of ropes, Patrick looked out and saw the car of his wife, Christen Patrick, about a quarter-mile away at an Exxon station, where a crowd of nearly 100 people had gathered to watch the rescue. He gave her a high-altitude FaceTime call that the two of them and their kids will never forget.
Patrick, Winchell, Pointer and the other rescuers on the tower heard two explosions of cheers: one at 12:24 p.m. when James set foot on the ground, and another 18 minutes later when Reynolds stepped off the tower. “Get me out of this harness right now!” a relieved Reynolds said when her shoes touched earth.
Both balloonists were taken to Longview Regional Medical Center. They were just fine physically and were soon released—Reynolds that afternoon and James, given his age, the following morning. But the work on the tower wasn’t over quite yet.
“As soon as the survivors got on the ground, my stress level actually increased tremendously,” Johnson says, “because I knew that we had 14 guys still up on the tower who were mentally, physically and emotionally exhausted.” One by one, the rescuers clip-climbed down the ladder, with food, hydration and hugs waiting for them when they reunited with their colleagues on the ground.
The firefighters who were on duty that day headed back to the station to await the next emergency call. Patrick, whose day off had been interrupted, took his family out for a late lunch at Panda Express and then spent a busy night fielding calls and texts from family and friends who had seen him on the news.
Despite her terrifying experience, Reynolds isn’t ready to give up ballooning. James, on the other hand, says he’s done. But after nearly 500 flights, he’s fine with that. James and Reynolds have accepted an open invitation to visit the firehouse and have grown close with the firefighters. “We’ve brought them into our family,” Johnson says.
After the balloon was carefully cut away from the tower and lowered to the ground, James donated the basket and part of the canopy to the Longview Fire Department. They now hang from the ceiling of the station. Says Patrick, “It’s a reminder of why we train—even for things we may hope and think we’ll never have to do.”

Next, it was James’s turn. He hooked his harness onto the line, stepped to the edge of the basket, turned his back to the tower and made his way across, his body swinging in the wind. Then Winchell grabbed hold of him and steered him into the tower. At 10:58 a.m., a little less than three hours after the balloon crashed, James and Reynolds were safe and secure, and thanking their rescuers profusely. But they still had 900 feet to go.

The firefighters’ plan was to lower James and Reynolds, still in their harnesses, a couple hundred feet at a time by hand, using ropes and pulleys. The rescuers agreed that the 73-year-old should get to the ground first, even though he was doing just fine physically. He also had family, including Lori and Lindsay, waiting below. The slow, careful descent began. At the first changeover point a couple hundred feet below, two firefighters hooked James into a safety clip attached to the tower, unclipped him from the first set of ropes and attached him to the second set.

“Have y’all ever done this before?” James asked the rescuers. “Yes,” came the response. “But not from this height.” Once James was on the second set of ropes, Reynolds began her descent. As the pair got closer to the ground, the mood turned lighter—at one of the stations, Capt. Clint Steelman told Reynolds he was hungry and asked if she had a cheeseburger.

Once James and Reynolds completed the transition off the first set of ropes, Patrick looked out and saw the car of his wife, Christen Patrick, about a quarter-mile away at an Exxon station, where a crowd of nearly 100 people had gathered to watch the rescue. He gave her a high-altitude FaceTime call that the two of them and their kids will never forget.

Patrick, Winchell, Pointer and the other rescuers on the tower heard two explosions of cheers: one at 12:24 p.m. when James set foot on the ground, and another 18 minutes later when Reynolds stepped off the tower. “Get me out of this harness right now!” a relieved Reynolds said when her shoes touched earth.

Both balloonists were taken to Longview Regional Medical Center. They were just fine physically and were soon released—Reynolds that afternoon and James, given his age, the following morning. But the work on the tower wasn’t over quite yet.

“As soon as the survivors got on the ground, my stress level actually increased tremendously,” Johnson says, “because I knew that we had 14 guys still up on the tower who were mentally, physically and emotionally exhausted.” One by one, the rescuers clip-climbed down the ladder, with food, hydration and hugs waiting for them when they reunited with their colleagues on the ground.

The firefighters who were on duty that day headed back to the station to await the next emergency call. Patrick, whose day off had been interrupted, took his family out for a late lunch at Panda Express and then spent a busy night fielding calls and texts from family and friends who had seen him on the news.

Despite her terrifying experience, Reynolds isn’t ready to give up ballooning. James, on the other hand, says he’s done. But after nearly 500 flights, he’s fine with that. James and Reynolds have accepted an open invitation to visit the firehouse and have grown close with the fire­fighters. “We’ve brought them into our family,” Johnson says.

After the balloon was carefully cut away from the tower and lowered to the ground, James donated the basket and part of the canopy to the Longview Fire Department. They now hang from the ceiling of the station. Says Patrick, “It’s a reminder of why we train—even for things we may hope and think we’ll never have to do.”

articles.content:
Fact: We know that nearly all last names in the United States—a whopping 97%!—are passed down to us from our fathers. But how surnames were actually created and when they became a tradition is more complex story.
“Names can be endlessly fascinating, as they hold special significance as emblems of our identity,” says Nathaniel Taylor, PhD, president of the American Society of Genealogists. “We can look at the names of our ancestors or others in our societies stretching back hundreds or even thousands of years.”
Then there’s the staggering variety of last names in the U.S. alone, with 7.8 million different ones currently in use, per the 2020 census. Just 11 of these names were reported more than a million times each, while the vast majority, 7 million, were counted fewer than 100 times.
My own last name at birth was Kelly, a common Irish one that means “descendant of Ceallach.” Aside from some grade-school teasing (“Smelly Kelly!”), I loved it. But when I got married, I took on a more challenging one: Geddes. Not many know its origins (Scotland) or meaning (mountain ridge), and fewer still can pronounce it—Geddes rhymes with lettuce. But at least there’s no silly taunting!
So what are the most common last names in the U.S. today, and how did they come to be? To find out, we turned to Taylor and Crista Cowan, Ancestry’s corporate genealogist. Read on to learn their origins and get a few clues about how your last name may have gotten its start too.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, history, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Believe it or not, no. In fact, in the Western world, for thousands of years, people simply went by one name—their first. But eventually, the need for surnames became apparent, since too many folks had the same first names. “Surnames are a medieval invention in Europe, appearing in many parts of the region from the 11th to the 13th centuries,” Taylor explains. “European-style inherited surnames came to the Western Hemisphere later on, between the 16th and 17th centuries.”
Experts believe the earliest recorded European last name is “O Cleirigh,” which originated in Ireland in 916 AD and would be spelled O’Clery today. But the Chinese have that record beat! “China developed hereditary family names, called Xing, more than 3,000 years ago, which makes its surname tradition one of the oldest in the world,” explains Cowan.
Other ancient cultures tracked lineage through titles or sacred roles rather than fixed last names. “For instance,” Cowan says, “Jewish Kohanim (priestly lines tracing back to Aaron, Moses’s brother) kept track of their hereditary lineage for thousands of years, even though fixed European surnames for these families, like Katz, which is short for Kohen Tsedek, were only formalized much later in history.”
Along with the need to distinguish all the different people named John or Mary, last names took off because of big jumps in population, an increase in the number and types of trades, and the use of written records. Wealth and social prestige were also behind their rise. “The factors that gave rise to inheriting a surname included new laws about marriage and property inheritance in 12th-century Europe,” Taylor says.
Other motives were cultural, Taylor adds, as families were organized around a father-to-son legacy of status and identity. The result? Surnames served as visual symbols like coats of arms.
Many of the last names we use in the U.S. today originated along five different, and surprisingly simple, paths. For the most part, these categories developed between the 12th and 14th centuries, though there are some variations in the chronology in different cultural traditions.
Keep in mind that the idea of surnames wasn’t exactly a conscious choice by a parent. “When surnames first appear in the written records, it’s because someone else described the person they were writing about in a certain way,” Taylor says. “So the ‘invention’ of many surnames may have been accidental moments in recordkeeping.”
With that in mind, here are the most common ways last names were born.
A patronymic—a term derived from the Greek words for father and name—is a name created with a prefix or suffix attached to a father or male relative’s moniker. Typically of Germanic, Scandinavian, Celtic, Hispanic and Slavic origin, many of these common last names are easy to spot since they sport son at the end (think: Williamson, Johnson, Wilson or Richardson) or prefixes (like O’Brian or O’Neill and MacDonald or McNamara). The Spanish suffix ez also means “son”; examples of these last names include Lopez, Sanchez, Fernandez and Alvarez.
While less common, women also passed down matronymics, such as Nelson (which is derived from Nell or Eleanor), Emmett (Emma), Madison (Maude) and Marriott (Mary). “In parts of South Asia (India, Indonesia), there are cultures where matrilineal inheritance of surnames is the rule,” says Taylor.
Names describing the jobs a person held were also a frequent way of making surnames. If you crafted barrels, you might be designated as a Cooper, and if you worked with sheep, you’d be called a Shepherd. Baker, Miller, Carpenter, Fisher and Taylor are other occupations that morphed into last names.
While it might not seem very politically correct today, one’s appearance, personality or nickname became, in some cases, that person’s last name. Examples of these descriptors include Armstrong, Longfellow, Brown, Little, Russo (red), LeBlanc (white), Young, Stern, Swift and Wise.
The landscape was also a source of inspiration when creating last names in medieval times. “These are sometimes called toponymic surnames,” Taylor says. “They encompassed features found in many locales, which then gave rise to unrelated families using the same surname.” Some common location-based names include Hill, Wood, Dupont (French for “from the bridge”), Stone, Atwater, Ford, Vega (Spanish for “meadow” or “fertile plain”) and Cumberland.
Where a person lived also prompted some surnames, including Sussex, Sutton, Kensington and Huntington. And if you owned property, your last name night be the same as your estate’s name. The British royal family, Windsor, is a prime example of this, along with other noble monikers such as Spencer and Stuart.
“In English history, you see names from big historic noble families like Howard, Seymour and Percy,” Cowan says. “Across Europe, noble family names often used little prefixes like de in French or Spanish or von in German, like de Medici or von Habsburg, to show that the family ruled over or owned a specific area.”
Similar to the folks who acquired their surnames based on their occupation, people who held jobs on these grand properties were often identified by those jobs. “So you get names like Reeve or Bailiff for estate managers, Granger for the person in charge of the granary, Hayward for the officer protecting hedges and boundaries, and Bond or Freeman, which shows whether someone was a peasant bound to the land or a free tenant farmer,” Cowan says.
It’s important to remember that not all cultures hewed to the paths outlined above. “Across many African, Indigenous and South Asian traditions, surnames grew out of clan lineages, spiritual titles or personal characteristics,” Cowan notes.

How many there are in the U.S.: 2,369,644

How many there are in the U.S.: 1,561,395

How many there are in the U.S.: 1,386,083
Meaning: Similar to Jon or Jone, this English and Welsh last name was created to denote a person who lived or worked at John’s house.
How many there are in the U.S.: 1,383,250
Meaning: Garcia has both Spanish and Portuguese roots and may come from the Basque area. It translates to “young bear” or “brave warrior.”
How many there are in the U.S.: 1,149,510

How many there are in the U.S.: 1,129,186

How many there are in the U.S.: 1,085,838
Meaning: Also a patronymic, Davis is English and Welsh and translates to “son of David.”
How many there are in the U.S.: 1,074,448

How many there are in the U.S.: 1,039,848
Probably not, especially if the last name is common. Still, as science improves, this answer might change. “Over the last 25 years, DNA databases have shown some trends about the likelihood that holders of the same surname are related biologically,” Taylor says. However, if your name is on the unusual side, the chances are better that you’ve got kin around the world. “The rarer the surname, the more likely it is that there is only one biological family accounting for it—only one founding ancestor,” he explains.
My own last name just might fall in the latter basket. “Geddes, per online sources, is indeed that sort of name: a geographically derived surname probably from a single place in Nairnshire, Scotland,” says Taylor. Interesting!
The sky’s the limit when it comes to adding last names. Indeed, as with first names, creating new last names is potentially an endless creative process. You can literally choose what you want for yourself and your offspring. “Dual surnames and hyphenated names are way more visible now, partly because of long-standing cultural norms like Hispanic dual-surname traditions, and partly because modern couples are choosing to blend or keep their names,” Cowan says. “It’s a great reminder that surnames aren’t static; they keep growing to reflect who we actually are.”
Taylor agrees. “With the convergence of so many distinct cultures in a melting pot like ours and the ability to borrow from cultures, the opportunity for new surnames and new patterns is greater than ever before,” he says.
Alas, tracking the wide range of last names isn’t as easy as first names. Thanks to the Social Security Administration, we have an excellent database that traces baby-name choice. “But,” Taylor says, “there’s no similar handy statistical source for surname use in America.”

articles.title: We Asked 45 People Over 80 About the Secret to Happiness—And They All Wished They’d Known This One Thing Earlier
articles.content:
Today I have answered 500(ish) emails, sent 300 texts, driven five teenagers to the mall, cleaned up four piles of dog vomit, taught three fitness classes, done two interviews, written one-and-a-half articles, attended one Spanish class … and it’s not even dinnertime yet. All that’s missing is the partridge in a pear tree. So my life is certainly full. But is it fulfilling? I can’t exactly say that all these things today brought me joy. But if we want to be Truly Happy aren’t we supposed to be, like, finding joy in the little things? Or something?
It’s that “or something” that I think about a lot these days, as the days fly by ever faster. Where are we supposed to find that happiness for our “one beautiful life” when it’s just so dang busy? Then it occurred to me that while we’ll ask 500 strangers online how to do sourdough bread, for some reason we never ask the people who’ve been doing this life thing for 80 years or more how to do life. Thankfully, I can fill that gap for all of us.
I write the 100 Years Strong column for The Healthy, where I interview people in their 80s, 90s and 100s about their lives and longevity secrets. I make it a point to ask each one what their secret to happiness is. And make no mistake: These people are happy happy. Even though they’ve lived through the Great Depression, World War II, the Civil Rights Movement, multiple revolutions in other countries and the full gamut of difficult personal challenges, nearly all of them are pretty positive most of the time.
“That doesn’t surprise me one bit. People do tend to get happier as they get older,” says Robert Waldinger, MD, a psychiatrist and the co-director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, the longest-running study of happiness in the world. If there’s one person who has interviewed more elderly folks than I have, it’s definitely him. “It’s a real, documented thing, called the positivity effect,” he explains. “There’s a psychological shift around the mid-40s, when people begin to realize life is short.”
To help find out what makes people happy, I interviewed more than 45 people, aged 80 to 103, and asked them what they wish they’d understood about happiness sooner and what keeps them smiling. Read on to find out. The answer will definitely surprise you—it’s basically the opposite of what the self-help section says.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more happiness, life advice, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The hard-earned secret that comes up most often among our folks can be best summed up by 100-year-old Dwight Roberts: “I don’t even think of life in terms of happiness. My mind doesn’t work on that level.”

Of course not! You’ll have days when you don’t feel happy, weeks when your plans fall apart and stretches when finding the energy to do much of anything feels harder than usual. That’s being human, not failing at happiness. The point isn’t to be cheerful all the time. It’s to keep making room for connection, curiosity and things that give your life meaning—even when you’re having a rough patch.

And it’s never too late to start something new. Just ask Natalie Grabow, our 80-year-old Ironman champion.

“I didn’t even learn to swim until I was 59 years old!” she tells me. “People think motivation fades with age. But if anything, it gets clearer.”

Maybe that’s the real secret: You don’t have to figure out how to be happy forever. In fact, there’s no such thing as happiness forever. Instead, keep living, keep connecting with others, stay aware of what does make you happy and stay open to whatever tomorrow brings.
